newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - BT seen unbowed by RWE blow.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BT seen unbowed by RWE blow.

text.p: The decision by German utility RWE to sever links with British Telecommunications (BT) will not damage the British giant's ambitious expansion plans in Germany, Europe's largest telecom market, analysts said on Thursday.

Most dismissed Wednesday's strategic reshuffle that broke RWE's links with BT and its partner Viag, another German utility. RWE instead opted to join a rival consortium led by Cable & Wireless and Germany's Veba.

"We're not at all worried about BT's prospects in Germany," said one leading analyst who declined to be named. "We recognise in terms of sentiment that it first sounded like a blow. But in the long run, we're quite happy with BT's strategy in Germany."

With the departure of RWE, BT also loses the energy company's 4,500 km (2,796 mile) fibre optic network in northern Germany. In contrast, Munich-based Viag covers only about 40 percent of the population.

Cable and Wireless, which is the main shareholder in BT's telecoms rival in Britain, Mercury, gets about 450 million marks ($294 million) as its share of the overcapitalised new alliance and will see its share of the start-up costs in Germany slashed.

Analysts expect C&W, which says the combined network of Veba and RWE gives it access to about 67 percent of the German population, to be able to show an extra profit of about 50-100 million pounds ($78-$156 million) for 1998.

Nevertheless, most analysts favoured BT, with its operations in 30 countries, as a stronger contender for a slice of the lucrative German market when the Deutsche Telekom monopoly is opened to full competition in 1998.
"BT is clearly one of the world's best operators in the competitive environment," noted another analyst.

Competing against soon-to-be-privatised Deutsche Telekom was more about providing service -- through mobile phones, voice telephony and seamless corporate and data services -- than engineering, analysts said.

"On the one side BT have done the right thing, because RWE had bigger ideas in terms of investment and BT's view is that it isn't necessary to go out and buy a lot of capacity when you can just rent it and offer people services like Concert," said Mike Stiles, telecoms analyst at Credit Lyonnais Laing.
Concert, which provides international voice and data services, is a joint venture between BT and America's MCI Communications Corp.
BT's strategy is to move into Germany by linking up with other networks and reaching residential customers through the fourth mobile phone licence without digging up the streets.
The C&W consortium is more interested in large-scale infrastrucure investments -- ranked as less prudent by analysts.
"If you look at the UK market, where there has been a proliferation of infrastructure, it is the people who are owning the new infrastructure who are really struggling.
"Those who are in a position to be able to buy trunking, which is increasingly a commodity, are able to increase their margins," said another analyst, who declined to be named.

Until now, the main threat to Deutsche Telekom seemed to be coming from the DBKom alliance of Mannesmann AG, the German railway Deutsche Bahn AG and AT&T Corp, which is setting up a second national telecommunications network. ($1=1.5315 Mark) ($1=.6395 Pound)
